newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's PRI takes legal steps to keep majority.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's PRI takes legal steps to keep majority.

text.p: Mexico's ruling party has made a last-ditch attempt to retain its 68-year control of the lower house of Congress, by disputing a string of results from the July 6 mid-term elections.
A high-ranking member of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) said on Friday that the PRI would challenge the results of scores of congressional races.
"There are legal bases for overturning some results and reaching an absolute majority in the Chamber of Deputies," Ricardo Monreal, legal coordinator of the PRI told reporters.
In the mid-term elections in which the PRI suffered its worst setback since it took power in 1929, it won 239 seats in the lower house, 12 seats short of the 251 it needed for a majority.
Late on Thursday, PRI officials presented electoral authorities with a stack of documents they said were aimed at proving electoral "irregularities" in 77 different cases.
Opposition parties have also contested results in 127 cases, and the Electoral Tribunal, the final arbiter of the results, has until Aug. 23 to decide if any are invalid.
The new Chamber of Deputies is due to open on Sept. 1.
According to the Tribunal's head, Jose Luis de la Peza, some 85 percent of the PRI's complaints or irregularities relate to opposition wins in the lower house.
But De la Peza said that after presidential elections in 1994, almost 80 percent of the challenges were rejected for lack of evidence. The July 6 vote was considered the cleanest in Mexican history.
In past elections, most of the post-election challenges came from opposition parties, who accused the PRI of using fraud to maintain its grip on power.
